computer/alu.title: ALU
computer/alu.content:
ALU stands for Arithmetic Logic Unit.
It is a part of the CPU that performs calculations and logical operations.
Main Operations
The ALU can perform:

addition
subtraction
comparison
AND
OR
NOT
bit shifting

Key Idea
The ALU is responsible for arithmetic and logic operations inside the CPU.

computer/bit-byte.title: Bits and Bytes
computer/bit-byte.content:
A bit is the smallest unit of digital information.
A bit can have one of two values:
0 or 1
Byte
A byte is a group of 8 bits.
1 byte = 8 bits
For example:
10110110
is one byte.
Common Units
1 byte (B)  = 8 bits
1 KB        ≈ 1,000 bytes
1 MB        ≈ 1,000 KB
1 GB        ≈ 1,000 MB
1 TB        ≈ 1,000 GB
Bits are usually written with a lowercase b, while bytes use an uppercase B.
Mb = megabits
MB = megabytes
What Does 64-Bit Mean?
Most modern personal computers use a 64-bit processor and operating system.
The bit value commonly refers to the width of the processor’s registers, addresses, and instructions.
How to Check on macOS
From Terminal, you can run:
uname -m
Common results include:
arm64  → 64-bit Apple silicon
x86_64 → 64-bit Intel processor

computer/bus.title: Bus
computer/bus.content:
A bus is a group of wires or signal lines used to transfer information between computer components.
A bus can carry:

data
addresses
control signals

Main Types
Data Bus
The data bus carries actual data between components.
For example, it can transfer data between the CPU and memory.
Address Bus
The address bus carries the location of the data.
It tells the system which memory address or device should be accessed.
Control Bus
The control bus carries commands and timing signals.
Examples:

read
write
clock
interrupt

Example
When the CPU reads data from memory:

The address bus selects a memory location.
The control bus sends a read signal.
The data bus transfers the stored data to the CPU.

Key Idea
A bus allows the CPU, memory, and other devices to communicate with each other.

computer/control-unit.title: Control Unit
computer/control-unit.content:
The Control Unit is a part of the CPU that directs how an instruction is executed.
It reads the instruction and generates control signals that tell other components what to do.
Main Role
The Control Unit can control:

the ALU
registers
memory
multiplexers
the program counter

For example, it determines whether the CPU should:

perform an ALU operation
read from memory
write to memory
store a result in a register
branch to another instruction

Control Signals
In a RISC-V processor, common control signals include:

RegWrite
MemRead
MemWrite
MemToReg
ALUSrc
ALUOp
Branch

The values of these signals depend mainly on the instruction’s opcode.
Example
For an addition instruction:
add x3, x1, x2
the Control Unit tells the CPU to:

read x1 and x2
send both values to the ALU
perform addition
write the result into x3

Simple Diagram
Instruction
    ↓
┌────────────────┐
│  Control Unit  │
└────────────────┘
   ↓    ↓    ↓
 ALU  Memory  Registers
Key Idea
The Control Unit does not perform the calculation itself.
It generates the signals that coordinate the datapath and make the instruction execute correctly.

computer/cpu.title: CPU
computer/cpu.content:
CPU stands for Central Processing Unit.
It is the main processor of a computer.
The CPU executes instructions and controls other parts of the system.
Main Parts
Control Unit
The control unit manages the execution of instructions.
It tells other components what to do.
ALU
The ALU performs calculations and logical operations.
Registers
Registers are very small and fast storage locations inside the CPU.
They hold data, instructions, and intermediate results.
How It Works
The CPU repeatedly:

fetches an instruction from memory
decodes the instruction
executes the instruction

This process is called the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
Key Idea
The CPU processes instructions, performs calculations, and controls the operation of a computer system.

computer/dram.title: DRAM
computer/dram.content:
DRAM stands for Dynamic Random Access Memory.
DRAM is commonly used as the main memory in computers and electronic devices.
How It Works
Each DRAM cell stores one bit of data using:

one transistor
one capacitor

The capacitor gradually loses its electrical charge, so the data must be refreshed repeatedly.
This is why it is called dynamic memory.
Main Uses

computers
smartphones
servers
graphics cards
embedded systems

Types of DRAM
SDRAM
SDRAM stands for Synchronous Dynamic Random Access Memory.
It operates in synchronization with the system clock, which allows memory operations to be coordinated with the processor.
DDR SDRAM
DDR stands for Double Data Rate.
It transfers data on both the rising and falling edges of the clock signal, allowing more data to be transferred per clock cycle.
Newer generations generally provide higher bandwidth and improved power efficiency.
LPDDR
LPDDR stands for Low-Power Double Data Rate.
It is designed to consume less power than standard DDR memory.
It is commonly used in:

smartphones
tablets
laptops
mobile devices

GDDR
GDDR stands for Graphics Double Data Rate.
It is designed for high-bandwidth graphics processing.
It is commonly used in:

graphics cards
gaming consoles
GPUs

HBM
HBM stands for High Bandwidth Memory.
It stacks multiple DRAM dies vertically and uses a very wide interface to transfer large amounts of data quickly.
HBM has become especially important because AI processors need extremely high memory bandwidth.
SK hynix, a Korean semiconductor company and a major HBM manufacturer, has gained significant market attention as demand for AI chips and HBM has increased.
It is commonly used in:

high-performance GPUs
AI accelerators
supercomputers

computer/dsp.title: DSP
computer/dsp.content:
DSP
DSP stands for Digital Signal Processor.
It is a processor designed to quickly perform mathematical operations on digital signals.
Signals
Real-world signals may include:

sound
voice
images
video
temperature
pressure
position

These signals are usually analog.
An ADC converts the analog signal into digital data before it is processed by the DSP.
How It Works
Analog signal
     ↓
ADC
     ↓
DSP
     ↓
DAC
     ↓
Analog output
The DSP processes the digital data using operations such as:

addition
subtraction
multiplication
filtering
compression
encoding and decoding

A DAC can then convert the processed digital signal back into an analog signal.
Example
In an audio player:

A microphone captures an analog sound signal.
An ADC converts it into digital data.
The DSP processes or compresses the audio.
The data is saved in memory.
During playback, the DSP decodes the audio.
A DAC converts it back into an analog signal for the speaker.

Main Components
A DSP usually includes:

Program Memory

Stores the program used to process signals.


Data Memory

Stores the signal data being processed.


Compute Engine

Performs mathematical operations.


Input and Output

Connects the DSP to memory, sensors, converters, and other devices.

computer/flash-memory.title: Flash Memory
computer/flash-memory.content:
Flash memory is a type of non-volatile memory.
It keeps stored data even when the power is turned off.
Main Uses

SSDs
smartphones
USB drives
memory cards
embedded systems

Types

NAND Flash
NOR Flash

Key Idea
Flash memory can be electrically erased and rewritten.
NAND Flash provides higher storage capacity, while NOR Flash provides faster random access.

computer/gpu.title: GPU
computer/gpu.content:
GPU stands for Graphics Processing Unit.
It is a processor designed to perform many calculations at the same time.
Main Uses
GPUs are commonly used for:

graphics rendering
video processing
gaming
AI and machine learning
scientific computing

How It Works
A CPU usually has a small number of powerful cores.
A GPU has many smaller cores that can process large amounts of similar data in parallel.
This makes GPUs efficient for tasks such as:

drawing pixels
processing images
matrix calculations
training AI models

GPU vs. CPU

























GPUCPUMany smaller coresFewer powerful coresGood at parallel tasksGood at general-purpose tasksUsed for graphics and AIUsed to control and run programsProcesses many similar operations at onceHandles different types of instructions
Key Idea
A GPU is designed for parallel processing.
It is especially useful when the same type of calculation must be repeated many times.

computer/mcu.title: MCU
computer/mcu.content:
MCU stands for Microcontroller Unit.
It is a small computer built into a single integrated circuit and is designed to control a specific electronic system.
Main Components
An MCU usually includes:

CPU
RAM
Flash memory
input and output pins
timers
communication interfaces
analog-to-digital converters

Main Uses
MCUs are commonly used in:

home appliances
automobiles
robots
sensors
IoT devices
embedded systems

How It Works
The program is stored in Flash memory.
The CPU executes the program, reads input signals, and controls connected devices through output pins.
For example, an MCU can:

read a temperature sensor
control a motor
turn an LED on or off
communicate with another device

Key Idea
An MCU combines processing, memory, and input/output functions into one chip.
It is mainly used to run embedded software and control electronic devices.

computer/memory.title: Memory
computer/memory.content:
Different types of memory are designed for different purposes, such as fast temporary access or long-term storage.
Volatile Memory
Volatile memory loses stored data when the power is turned off.

SRAM
DRAM

It is mainly used for temporary working data.
Non-Volatile Memory
Non-volatile memory keeps stored data even when the power is turned off.

ROM
Flash Memory
EEPROM

It is mainly used for long-term storage and firmware.
Memory Hierarchy
Memory is usually organized by speed, capacity, and cost.
From fastest to slowest:

CPU registers
cache
DRAM
storage

Faster memory is usually smaller and more expensive.
Key Idea
A computer uses multiple types of memory together.
Fast memory stores active data close to the processor, while slower non-volatile memory stores data for long-term use.

computer/nand-flash.title: NAND Flash
computer/nand-flash.content:
NAND Flash is a type of Flash Memory mainly used for data storage.

high storage capacity
low cost per bit
compact size

Main Uses

SSDs
smartphones
USB drives
memory cards

Key Idea
NAND Flash is suitable for storing large amounts of data, but it is generally slower than DRAM.

computer/nor-flash.title: NOR Flash
computer/nor-flash.content:
NOR Flash
NOR Flash is a type of Flash Memory mainly used for storing program code and firmware.
Main Uses

firmware
boot code
embedded systems
microcontrollers

Key Idea
NOR Flash allows fast random access, so a processor can read and execute code directly from it.
Compared with NAND Flash, NOR Flash is usually faster for reading small amounts of data, but it is more expensive and has lower storage capacity.

computer/register.title: Register
computer/register.content:
A register is a very small and fast storage location inside a CPU.
It temporarily holds data that the processor is currently using.
Main Uses
Registers can store:

numbers
instructions
memory addresses
calculation results

Examples

Program Counter

Stores the address of the next instruction.


Instruction Register

Stores the current instruction.


General-Purpose Register

Stores temporary data and calculation results.



Key Idea
Registers are the fastest type of memory in a computer.
They are small in capacity but allow the CPU to access data very quickly.

computer/rom.title: ROM
computer/rom.content:
ROM stands for Read-Only Memory.
ROM is mainly used to store data that changes rarely, such as firmware and boot instructions.
Main Uses

firmware
boot code
embedded systems
device configuration
microcontrollers

Types of ROM
PROM
PROM stands for Programmable Read-Only Memory.
It is manufactured without stored data and can be programmed once by the user.
After programming, the data cannot be erased.
EPROM
EPROM stands for Erasable Programmable Read-Only Memory.
It can be erased using ultraviolet light and then programmed again.
The chip usually has a transparent window that allows ultraviolet light to reach the memory cells.
EEPROM
EEPROM stands for Electrically Erasable Programmable Read-Only Memory.
It can be erased and rewritten electrically without removing it from the device.
It is commonly used for storing:

configuration settings
calibration values
small amounts of persistent data

Flash Memory
Flash Memory is a type of EEPROM.
It erases and writes data in larger blocks, making it faster and more suitable for larger storage capacities.
The two main types are:

NAND Flash
NOR Flash

Key Features

non-volatile
stores permanent or rarely changed data
generally slower to write than RAM
suitable for firmware and boot code

Key Idea
ROM stores data that must remain available even when a device is turned off.
Modern systems often use EEPROM or Flash Memory instead of traditional fixed ROM.

computer/sram.title: SRAM
computer/sram.content:
SRAM stands for Static Random Access Memory.
SRAM is faster than DRAM and is mainly used for small, high-speed memory.
How It Works
An SRAM cell stores one bit of data using several transistors, commonly six.
Unlike DRAM, SRAM does not need to be refreshed while power is supplied.
This is why it is called static memory.
Main Uses

CPU cache
processor registers
buffers
networking devices
embedded systems

Key Features

very fast
does not require refreshing
more expensive than DRAM
lower storage density
volatile

Key Idea
SRAM is used when very fast memory access is more important than capacity or cost.

computer/ssd.title: SSD
computer/ssd.content:
SSD stands for Solid-State Drive.
It is a storage device that uses Flash Memory to store data.
Main Uses
SSDs store:

operating systems
applications
documents
photos
videos

How It Works
An SSD stores data in NAND Flash memory.
A controller manages where data is written, read, and erased.

computer/thread-scheduling.title: Thread Scheduling
computer/thread-scheduling.content:
What is Thread Scheduling?
Thread scheduling is the process of deciding the order in which threads use the CPU.
Since multiple threads may be ready to run at the same time, the operating system needs a scheduling policy to decide which thread gets CPU time first, how long it runs, and when another thread should run.

Types of Thread Scheduling
1. Preemptive Scheduling
Preemptive scheduling is a scheduling method where the operating system can forcibly stop the currently running thread and assign the CPU to another thread.
In this method, a thread does not necessarily run until it finishes. Instead, the operating system may interrupt it depending on the scheduling policy.
Examples of preemptive scheduling policies include:

Round Robin
Priority-Based Scheduling
Shortest Job First

Advantages
Preemptive scheduling allows the CPU to be shared more dynamically among multiple threads. This can improve responsiveness and make the system feel faster, especially when many threads are running.
Disadvantages
Because threads may be switched frequently, context switching costs occur. A context switch takes time because the system must save the current thread’s state and load another thread’s state.

2. Non-Preemptive Scheduling
Non-preemptive scheduling is a scheduling method where once a thread gets the CPU, it continues using the CPU until it finishes or voluntarily gives up control.
In this method, the operating system does not forcibly interrupt the running thread.
Advantages
Non-preemptive scheduling is simpler to implement and does not cause frequent context switching costs.
Disadvantages
It may be difficult to use the CPU efficiently when multiple threads are waiting. If one thread runs for a long time, other threads may have to wait for a long time before they can execute.

Thread States
1. New / Ready State
This is the state where a thread has been created and allocated in memory. The thread is ready to use the CPU, but it has not been assigned CPU time yet.
2. Running State
This is the state where a thread is currently using the CPU.
3. Not Runnable State
This is the state where a thread exists in memory but cannot currently use the CPU.
4. Dead / Terminated State
This is the state where a thread has finished its execution and is no longer active.
Related: Thread

computer/thread.title: Thread
computer/thread.content:
A thread is the smallest unit of execution inside a process.
A process can contain multiple threads, and each thread can run a different task. Threads in the same process share memory, which makes communication faster but also requires careful synchronization.
A thread allows a program to do multiple tasks at the same time.

A process is the whole running program.
A thread is a worker inside that process.

cybersecurity/cia-triad.title: CIA Triad
cybersecurity/cia-triad.content:
The CIA Triad is a basic cybersecurity model used to protect information.
CIA stands for:
Confidentiality

Only authorized people can access the information.

Example: using passwords, encryption, and access control to protect private data.
Integrity

Information should be accurate and not changed without permission.

Example: preventing someone from modifying a file or database record.
Availability

Systems and data should be accessible when needed.

Example: keeping a website online and preventing downtime from attacks or failures.

cybersecurity/computer-network.title: Computer Network
cybersecurity/computer-network.content:
A computer network is a group of connected devices that can communicate and share data with each other.
Examples of devices include computers, phones, servers, routers, and printers.
Main Purpose
Computer networks allow devices to:

share data
access the internet
communicate with servers
use shared resources like printers or files

Common Types

LAN

A local network in a small area, such as a home, school, or office.


WAN

A large network that connects devices across cities, countries, or the world.


Internet

The largest global network connecting millions of devices.



Important Components

Router

Sends data between different networks.


Switch

Connects devices within the same local network.


Server

Provides services or data to other devices.


Client

A device that requests data or services from a server.



Simple Example
When you open a website, your computer sends a request through the network to a web server.
The server sends the website data back to your computer.

cybersecurity/cryptography.title: Cryptography
cybersecurity/cryptography.content:
Cryptography is the practice of protecting information by converting it into a secure form.
It is used to keep data private, verify identities, and protect data from being changed.
Main Purposes

Confidentiality

Keeps information secret from unauthorized people.


Integrity

Makes sure data has not been changed.


Authentication

Verifies the identity of users, systems, or websites.


Non-repudiation

Prevents someone from denying that they performed an action.



Common Concepts

Encryption

Converts readable data into unreadable data.


Decryption

Converts encrypted data back into readable data.


Key

A secret value used to encrypt or decrypt data.


Hashing

Creates a fixed-size value from data to check integrity.



Simple Example
When a website uses HTTPS, cryptography helps protect passwords and personal information while they travel between the browser and the server.

cybersecurity/index.title: Cybersecurity
cybersecurity/index.content:
Cybersecurity is about understanding how systems break, how people make mistakes, and how to protect information from threats.
I became interested in cybersecurity through internship, and studying security fundamentals.
Related: CompTIA Security+

cybersecurity/defense-in-depth.title: Defense in Depth
cybersecurity/defense-in-depth.content:
Defense in Depth is a cybersecurity strategy that uses multiple layers of protection.
The idea is that if one security layer fails, other layers can still protect the system.
Examples of Security Layers

Firewall

Blocks suspicious network traffic.


Access Control

Limits who can access systems and data.


MFA

Adds extra verification during login.


Encryption

Protects data even if it is stolen.


Monitoring

Detects suspicious activity.


Backups

Helps recover data after an incident.



Simple Example
A company may use a firewall, strong passwords, MFA, antivirus software, and backups together.
Even if an attacker bypasses one layer, they still have to get through the others.

cybersecurity/risk-management.title: Risk Management
cybersecurity/risk-management.content:
Risk Management is the process of identifying, assessing, and reducing risks that could harm an organization.
In cybersecurity, risk usually means the chance that a threat will exploit a vulnerability and cause damage.
Main Steps

Identify Risks


Find possible threats, vulnerabilities, and assets that need protection.


Assess Risks


Understand how likely the risk is and how serious the impact would be.


Prioritize Risks


Focus on the risks that could cause the most damage.


Treat Risks


Decide how to handle the risk.

Risk Treatment Options

Avoid

Stop doing the risky activity.


Reduce

Add security controls to lower the risk.


Transfer

Share the risk with another party, such as insurance.


Accept

Accept the risk if it is low or unavoidable.



Simple Example
If a company stores customer data, there is a risk of data leakage.
The company can reduce this risk by using encryption, access control, and regular security monitoring.

cybersecurity/social-engineering.title: Social Engineering
cybersecurity/social-engineering.content:
Social Engineering is a cyberattack method that tricks people instead of attacking systems directly.
Attackers use human emotions like trust, fear, urgency, or curiosity to make people reveal sensitive information or take unsafe actions.
Common Examples

Phishing

Fake emails or messages that try to steal passwords or personal information.


Impersonation

Pretending to be someone trusted, like a coworker, manager, or IT support.


Pretexting

Creating a fake story to convince someone to share information.

cybersecurity/ssl-and-tls.title: SSL/TLS
cybersecurity/ssl-and-tls.content:
SSL/TLS is a security protocol used to protect data sent over the internet.
It is commonly used in HTTPS to secure communication between a browser and a web server.
SSL vs TLS

SSL stands for Secure Sockets Layer.
TLS stands for Transport Layer Security. TLS is the newer and more secure version of SSL.

Main Purposes

Encryption

Prevents others from reading the data.


Authentication

Verifies that the server is really who it claims to be.


Integrity

Ensures the data was not changed during transmission.



Simple Example
When a website uses https://, TLS helps protect sensitive data like passwords, payment information, and personal details.
Key Idea
SSL/TLS makes internet communication secure by encrypting data and verifying identities.

cybersecurity/vulnerability-management.title: Vulnerability Management
cybersecurity/vulnerability-management.content:
Vulnerability Management is the process of finding, assessing, prioritizing, and fixing security weaknesses in systems, applications, and networks.
The goal is to reduce the chance that attackers can exploit known vulnerabilities.
Main Steps

Identify


Scan systems to find vulnerabilities.


Assess


Understand how serious each vulnerability is.


Prioritize


Fix the most critical risks first.


Remediate


Patch, configure, or remove the vulnerable component.


Monitor


Continuously check for new vulnerabilities.

Key Idea
Not every vulnerability has the same risk.
Vulnerability management focuses on fixing the vulnerabilities that are most likely to cause real damage.
Simple Example
If a server has outdated software with a known security flaw, the team should patch it before attackers can exploit it.

cybersecurity/zero-trust.title: Zero Trust Model
cybersecurity/zero-trust.content:
Zero Trust Model is a cybersecurity model based on the idea of “Never trust, always verify.”
In traditional security, users inside the company network were often trusted. However, Zero Trust does not automatically trust anyone, even if they are inside the network.
The main principles are:

Never Trust, Always Verify

Every user and device must be verified before access is allowed.


Least Privilege Access

Users only get the minimum access they need.


Continuous Monitoring

User activity is constantly checked, even after login.



For example, even if an employee logs into a company system, Zero Trust may still check their password, MFA, device status, location, and access permissions.
In short, Zero Trust means every access request must be verified instead of automatically trusted.

electrical-engineering/circuit-analysis/.title: Bode Plot
electrical-engineering/circuit-analysis/.content:
A Bode plot shows how a circuit or system responds to different frequencies.
It consists of two graphs:

Magnitude plot → shows gain versus frequency
Phase plot → shows phase shift versus frequency

The frequency axis is usually logarithmic.
Magnitude Plot
The magnitude plot shows how much the circuit amplifies or attenuates a signal.
Gain is commonly expressed in decibels:
Gain_{dB} = 20\log_{10}|A|
Gain (dB)
   │─────────
   │         \
   │          \
   │           \
   └──────────────── Frequency
Phase Plot
The phase plot shows how much the output signal is shifted in phase compared with the input.
Phase
  0° ─────────
              \
               \
-90°            ─────
   └──────────────── Frequency
What Bode Plots Are Used For
Bode plots help determine:

gain
bandwidth
cutoff frequency
frequency response
Phase Margin
stability

Example: Amplifier
At low frequencies, an amplifier may have nearly constant gain.
As frequency increases, the gain eventually begins to decrease.
The −3 dB frequency is often used to define the amplifier’s bandwidth.
Feedback Systems
For a Feedback System, Bode plots are especially useful for analyzing stability.
The magnitude and phase of the loop gain are used to determine quantities such as:

gain margin
Phase Margin
risk of oscillation

Key Idea
A Bode plot shows how gain and phase change with frequency.
Bode Plot
├── Magnitude → How much?
└── Phase     → How much phase shift?

electrical-engineering/circuit-analysis/.title: KCL
electrical-engineering/circuit-analysis/.content:
Kirchhoff’s Current Law (KCL)
KCL: The total current entering a node equals the total current leaving the node.
In other words, charge does not disappear or build up at a node.
\sum I_{in} = \sum I_{out}
or
\sum I = 0
where currents entering can be positive and currents leaving can be negative.
Example
If 3 currents meet at one node:
I_1 = I_2 + I_3
This means the current coming into the node splits into two paths.
When to use KCL
Use KCL when analyzing nodes in a circuit.
KCL is the basis of nodal analysis.

Quick Comparison

electrical-engineering/circuit-analysis/.title: KVL
electrical-engineering/circuit-analysis/.content:
Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law (KVL)
KVL: The sum of all voltage rises and drops around a closed loop is zero.
Energy is conserved around a loop.
\sum V = 0
Example
For a simple loop with one voltage source and two resistors:
V_s - V_1 - V_2 = 0
so
V_s = V_1 + V_2
This means the source voltage is divided across the resistors.
When to use KVL
Use KVL when analyzing loops in a circuit.
KVL is the basis of mesh analysis.

Intuition

KVL: voltage gained and lost around a loop balances out.
KCL: what comes into a node must go out.

electrical-engineering/circuit-analysis/.title: Noise
electrical-engineering/circuit-analysis/.content:
Electrical noise is an unwanted signal that interferes with the intended voltage, current, or data in a circuit.
It can cause:

incorrect measurements
audio distortion
communication errors
unstable circuit behavior

Common Sources
Noise can come from:

switching regulators
motors
digital circuits
power supplies
electromagnetic interference
thermal motion inside components

Example
A sensor may produce a small voltage signal:
Desired signal: 1.00 V
Noise:          ±0.02 V
Measured value: 0.98–1.02 V
The noise makes the measurement less accurate.
Types of Noise
Thermal Noise
Thermal noise is caused by the random movement of electrons inside components.
Switching Noise
Switching noise is produced when transistors turn on and off quickly.
It is common in:

switching regulators
digital circuits
processors

Electromagnetic Interference
Electromagnetic interference, or EMI, occurs when electromagnetic energy from another device affects a circuit.
Reducing Noise
Noise can be reduced using:

capacitors
filters
shielding
grounding
shorter signal paths
careful circuit-board layout

electrical-engineering/circuit-analysis/.title: Pole and Zero
electrical-engineering/circuit-analysis/.content:
Poles and zeros describe how a circuit or system responds to different frequencies.
They come from the system’s transfer function.
Transfer Function
A transfer function can be written as:
H(s)=\frac{\text{Numerator}}{\text{Denominator}}
Zero
A zero is a value of (s) that makes the transfer function equal to zero.
Zeros come from the numerator.
Numerator = 0
    ↓
   Zero
A zero usually causes the magnitude response to increase in slope.
For a simple first-order zero:

magnitude slope changes by about +20 dB/decade
phase can increase by about +90°

Pole
A pole is a value of (s) that makes the denominator equal to zero.
Poles come from the denominator.
Denominator = 0
      ↓
     Pole
A pole usually causes the magnitude response to decrease in slope.
For a simple first-order pole:

magnitude slope changes by about −20 dB/decade
phase can decrease by about −90°

Example
For:
H(s)=\frac{1+s/\omega_z}{1+s/\omega_p}

(\omega_z) → zero frequency
(\omega_p) → pole frequency

The pole and zero change the shape of the Bode Plot.
Pole vs. Zero

























PoleZeroComes from denominatorComes from numeratorUsually decreases gain slopeUsually increases gain slopeAdds phase lagAdds phase leadCan affect stability stronglyCan improve or worsen response
Stability
Poles are especially important for feedback systems.
If poles are located in unstable regions, the system can oscillate or become unstable.
Poles and zeros also affect:

bandwidth
Phase Margin
frequency response
transient response

Key Idea
Pole → tends to reduce gain and add phase lag.
Zero → tends to increase gain and add phase lead.
Poles and zeros determine the shape and stability of a system’s frequency response.

electrical-engineering/electronic-device.title: Amplifier
electrical-engineering/electronic-device.content:
An amplifier is an electronic circuit that makes a signal stronger.
It takes a small input signal and produces a larger output signal containing the same basic information.
Small input signal
        ↓
    Amplifier
        ↓
Larger output signal
For example:
Input:  0.01 V audio signal
Output: 1.0 V audio signal
What Stronger Means
An amplifier may increase:

voltage
current
power

An amplifier does not create energy from nothing.
It uses energy from a power supply and controls that energy according to the input signal.
Input signal ──→ controls amplifier
Power supply ──→ provides energy
Output signal ─→ stronger signal
Gain
The amount of amplification is called gain.
Voltage gain is:
A_v=\frac{V_{\text{out}}}{V_{\text{in}}}
For example:
Vin  = 0.1 V
Vout = 2.0 V
 
Voltage gain = 2.0 / 0.1 = 20
The amplifier therefore has a voltage gain of 20.
Common Types
Operational Amplifier
An Operational Amplifier is mainly used to amplify and process voltage signals.
Depending on the surrounding circuit, it can add, subtract, compare, integrate, or filter signals.
Audio Amplifier
An Audio Amplifier amplifies audio-frequency signals.
It can make a weak signal powerful enough to drive headphones or a speaker.
Audio source
     ↓
Audio amplifier
     ↓
Speaker
RF Amplifier
An RF amplifier amplifies high-frequency signals used in wireless communication.
Common RF amplifiers include:

Power Amplifier

Strengthens a transmitted RF signal before it reaches the antenna.


Low-Noise Amplifier

Strengthens a weak received RF signal while adding as little noise as possible.



Sensor Amplifier
A sensor amplifier strengthens a small sensor signal so that an ADC or processor can measure it accurately.

electrical-engineering/electronic-device.title: Bandwidth
electrical-engineering/electronic-device.content:
In an amplifier or electronic circuit, bandwidth is the range of frequencies that the circuit can process properly.
\text{Bandwidth}=f_H-f_L
where:

fL is the lower cutoff frequency
fH is the upper cutoff frequency

For example:
Lower cutoff: 20 Hz
Upper cutoff: 20 kHz
 
Bandwidth = 20 kHz − 20 Hz
A wider bandwidth allows the circuit to process a wider range of signal frequencies.

electrical-engineering/electronic-device.title: Comparator
electrical-engineering/electronic-device.content:
A comparator is a circuit that compares two input voltages.
It has:

a non-inverting input, V+
an inverting input, V−
one output

If V+ > V− → output HIGH
If V+ < V− → output LOW
How It Works
A comparator changes its output depending on which input voltage is greater.
Sensor voltage ──→ V+
Reference voltage → V−
If the sensor voltage rises above the reference voltage, the output changes state.
Example
Suppose:
V+ = 3 V
V− = 2 V
Because V+ > V−, the output becomes HIGH.
If:
V+ = 1 V
V− = 2 V
the output becomes LOW.
Main Uses
Comparators are used for:

threshold detection
battery-level monitoring
zero-crossing detection
sensor interfaces
converting analog signals into digital states

electrical-engineering/electronic-device.title: Operational Amplifier
electrical-engineering/electronic-device.content:
An operational amplifier, or op-amp, is an electronic circuit that amplifies the voltage difference between two inputs.
It has:

a non-inverting input +
an inverting input −
one output

Non-inverting input (+) ─┐
                         ├── Op-Amp ── Output
Inverting input (−) ─────┘
The basic relationship is:
V_{out}=A(V_+-V_-)
where A is the open-loop voltage gain.
The open-loop gain is usually extremely large.
Main Uses
Op-amps can perform:

amplification
addition
subtraction
integration
differentiation
filtering
signal comparison

Ideal Op-Amp Rules
For an ideal op-amp operating with negative feedback:

No current flows into the inputs.

I_+=I_-=0

The two input voltages are approximately equal.

V_+\approx V_-
The output is limited by the positive and negative supply voltages. If the calculated output exceeds these limits, the op-amp saturates.
Common Op-Amp Configurations
Inverting Amplifier
The input signal is connected to the inverting terminal.
The output has the opposite polarity from the input.
V_{out}=-\frac{R_f}{R_{in}}V_{in}
Input → Inverting amplifier → Inverted output
Non-Inverting Amplifier
The input signal is connected to the non-inverting terminal.
The output has the same polarity as the input.
V_{out}=\left(1+\frac{R_f}{R_g}\right)V_{in}
Voltage Follower
A voltage follower connects the output directly to the inverting input.
V_{out}=V_{in}
It does not increase voltage, but it isolates two circuit stages and provides current drive.
Summing Amplifier
A summing amplifier combines multiple input voltages into one output.
For equal input resistors:
V_{out}=-\frac{R_f}{R}\left(V_1+V_2+\cdots+V_n\right)
It can be used for audio mixing and analog calculations.
Differential Amplifier
A differential amplifier amplifies the difference between two input voltages.
V_{out}=A(V_2-V_1)
It is useful for measuring a small signal while rejecting voltage common to both inputs.
Integrator
An integrator produces an output related to the accumulated input signal over time.
V_{out}=-\frac{1}{RC}\int V_{in},dt
It uses a capacitor in the feedback path.
Differentiator
A differentiator produces an output related to how quickly the input changes.
V_{out}=-RC\frac{dV_{in}}{dt}
It responds strongly to rapid changes in the input signal.
Comparator
A comparator compares two voltages without normal negative feedback.

If V+ > V−, the output moves toward the positive supply.
If V+ < V−, the output moves toward the negative supply.

It is commonly used for threshold detection.

electrical-engineering/electronic-device.title: Phase Margin
electrical-engineering/electronic-device.content:
Phase margin is a measure of how stable a negative-feedback system is.
It tells us how close the system is to oscillation.
How It Is Measured
Phase margin is measured at the frequency where the loop gain becomes:
|A\beta| = 1
or:
0\text{ dB}
At that frequency:
\text{Phase Margin} = 180^\circ + \text{Loop Phase}
For example, if the loop phase is:
-120^\circ
then:
PM = 60^\circ
Interpretation


Small phase margin

less stable
more overshoot and ringing
higher risk of oscillation



Moderate phase margin

good balance between stability and speed
around 45–60° is common



Large phase margin

more stable
less overshoot and ringing
may have lower bandwidth and slower response



Bandwidth Trade-Off
There is often a trade-off between Bandwidth and phase margin.
Higher Bandwidth
→ Faster response
→ Usually lower phase margin
→ More stability risk
 
Higher Phase Margin
→ More stable
→ Usually lower bandwidth
→ Slower response
Bode Plot
Phase margin is found using a Bode Plot.
Find where loop gain = 0 dB
          ↓
Check the phase
          ↓
Measure distance from -180°
          ↓
Phase Margin
Key Idea
Phase margin shows how much additional phase shift a feedback system can tolerate before becoming unstable.
The goal is usually not to maximize phase margin, but to find a good balance between stability, bandwidth, and response speed.

electrical-engineering/electronic-device.title: MOSFET
electrical-engineering/electronic-device.content:
MOSFET: Metal-Oxide-Semicondcutor Field-Effect Transistor
A MOSFET is a transistor that controls current using voltage.
1. MOSFET Terminals
A MOSFET is usually drawn as a 3-terminal device, but physically it has 4 terminals:

Gate
Source
Drain
Body

For many MOSFETs, the source and drain are physically symmetric.
However, in circuit operation, we call one side “source” and the other side “drain” depending on the applied voltages and current direction.
2. NMOS and PMOS Body Connection
NMOS
An NMOS transistor is usually built in a p-type body.
This p-type body can be:

p-substrate
p-well

For NMOS, the body is usually connected to the lowest voltage, normally ground (GND).
This helps keep the body-source junction reverse-biased.
PMOS
A PMOS transistor is usually built in an n-well.
For PMOS, the body is usually connected to the highest voltage, normally VDD.
This also helps keep the body-source junction reverse-biased.
3. MOSFET Operation Regions
A MOSFET has three main operation regions:

Cut-off
Triode / Linear
Saturation

4. Cut-off Region
In cut-off, the MOSFET is mostly off.
For NMOS:
[
V_{GS} < V_{TH}
]
The gate-to-source voltage is not large enough to strongly turn on the channel, so ideally no drain current flows.
In real devices, a very small leakage current can still flow.
5. Triode / Linear Region
In triode region, the MOSFET is on, but it behaves more like a voltage-controlled resistor.
For NMOS:
[
V_{GS} > V_{TH}
]
and
[
V_{DS} < V_{GS} - V_{TH}
]
In this region, the MOSFET has an on-resistance called:
[
R_{on}
]
This region is often used when the MOSFET acts like a switch or resistor.
6. Saturation Region
In saturation region, the MOSFET behaves more like a current source.
For NMOS:
[
V_{GS} > V_{TH}
]
and
[
V_{DS} > V_{GS} - V_{TH}
]
Ideally, once the MOSFET enters saturation, the drain current becomes almost constant even if (V_{DS}) increases.
This is very important in analog circuits because amplifiers need a stable operating current.
7. Why Saturation Matters in Analog Circuits
In analog design, we often want MOSFETs to operate in the saturation region.
The reason is that in saturation, the drain current is mainly controlled by (V_{GS}), not (V_{DS}).
So even if (V_{DS}) changes, the current stays relatively stable.
This makes it possible to define a stable DC operating point, and then analyze small AC signal changes around that point.
In simple terms:

DC analysis decides where the transistor sits.
AC analysis studies how the circuit responds to small changes around that point.

8. Three Important MOSFET Effects
Real MOSFETs are not ideal.
There are three important non-ideal effects:

Channel Length Modulation, CLM
Body Effect
Parasitic Capacitance

9. Channel Length Modulation, CLM
Ideally, in saturation, drain current should stay constant as (V_{DS}) increases.
But in real MOSFETs, the drain current slightly increases as (V_{DS}) increases.
This effect is called channel length modulation.
It becomes stronger when the channel length is shorter.
So from the CLM point of view, using a longer channel length can make the current source more ideal.
In equations, CLM is often modeled using (\lambda):
[
I_D = I_{D,sat}(1 + \lambda V_{DS})
]
The parameter (\lambda) represents how much the current increases with (V_{DS}).
10. Body Effect
The body effect happens when the body voltage is different from the source voltage.
For NMOS, the body is usually connected to ground.
If the source is also at ground, then:
[
V_{SB} = 0
]
So there is no body effect.
But if the source voltage is not equal to the body voltage, then:
[
V_{SB} \neq 0
]
The threshold voltage (V_{TH}) changes.
In simple terms:

Body effect means the body-source voltage changes the threshold voltage.

11. Parasitic Capacitance
Parasitic capacitance is unwanted capacitance that naturally appears inside the MOSFET.
Whenever two conductive regions are separated by an insulating material, capacitance can form.
In MOSFETs, parasitic capacitances can appear between terminals such as:

Gate–Source
Gate–Drain
Drain–Body
Source–Body

These capacitances are usually unwanted because they affect speed, delay, and coupling.
Parasitic capacitance is strongly affected by the transistor width.
Larger width usually creates larger parasitic capacitance.
12. DC Analysis
DC analysis finds the DC operating point of the circuit.
For example, in a common-source amplifier, if (V_{in}) is below (V_{TH}), the NMOS is off and almost no current flows.
Then:
[
V_{out} \approx V_{DD}
]
As (V_{in}) increases above (V_{TH}), the NMOS turns on, current flows through the resistor, and (V_{out}) starts to decrease.
To build an amplifier, we usually choose (V_{in}), (R_D), and the MOSFET size so that the transistor operates in saturation.
A key goal in analog design is:

Bias the transistors so they operate in the correct region, usually saturation.

13. AC Analysis
After the DC operating point is set, AC analysis studies how small input changes are amplified.
The MOSFET can be replaced by a small-signal model.
Important small-signal parameters include:
Transconductance
[
g_m
]
This tells how much the drain current changes when (V_{GS}) changes.
In simple terms:

(g_m) tells how strongly the MOSFET converts voltage change into current change.

Output Resistance
[
r_o
]
This comes from channel length modulation.
If CLM is small, (r_o) is large, and the MOSFET behaves more like an ideal current source.
Body Transconductance
[
g_{mb}
]
This comes from body effect.
It models how changes in (V_{BS}) affect the drain current.
Summary
A MOSFET is a voltage-controlled current device.
In digital circuits, it is often used as a switch.
In analog circuits, it is biased at a proper DC operating point and used as a controlled current source.
The most important analog idea is:

Set the MOSFET in saturation for DC bias, then use small-signal analysis to understand AC amplification.

electrical-engineering/electronic-device.title: Switching Converter
electrical-engineering/electronic-device.content:
A switching converter changes one DC voltage into another using rapidly switching transistors.
It stores and transfers energy using:

inductors
capacitors
diodes
transistors

Switching converters are commonly used as efficient Voltage Regulator.
Main Types
Buck Converter
A buck converter lowers voltage.
12 V → 5 V
Boost Converter
A boost converter raises voltage.
3.7 V → 5 V
Buck-Boost Converter
A buck-boost converter can raise or lower voltage.
Variable input → stable output
Advantages

high efficiency
low power loss
suitable for large voltage changes

Disadvantages

more complex than a linear regulator
produces switching noise
requires careful circuit layout

Key Idea
A switching converter efficiently changes voltage by repeatedly switching and transferring stored energy.

electrical-engineering/electronic-device.title: Voltage Regulator
electrical-engineering/electronic-device.content:
A voltage regulator is a circuit that keeps its output voltage stable even when the input voltage or load current changes.
For example:
Battery: 3.2–4.2 V
        ↓
Voltage regulator
        ↓
Stable 1.0 V for CPU
Without a regulator, too much voltage can damage a chip, while too little voltage can cause errors or shutdowns.
Why Voltage Changes
A regulator compensates when:

the battery voltage falls
the processor suddenly uses more current
the input power fluctuates
parts of the device turn on or off

Main Types
Linear Regulator
A linear regulator lowers voltage by releasing excess energy as heat.
3.3 V input → linear regulator → 1.8 V output
Advantages

simple
low electrical noise
inexpensive

Disadvantages

less efficient when the voltage difference is large
produces heat

Switching Regulator
A Switching Converter uses rapidly switching transistors, inductors, and capacitors to convert voltage efficiently.
Common types include:

buck converter
boost converter
buck-boost converter

Switching regulators are usually more efficient than linear regulators, but they are more complex and produce more electrical noise.

electrical-engineering/semiconductor/dac.title: ADC/DAC
electrical-engineering/semiconductor/dac.content:
ADC and DAC connect analog signals with digital systems.
Analog signal → ADC → Digital data
Digital data → DAC → Analog signal
ADC
ADC stands for Analog-to-Digital Converter.
It converts a continuous analog signal into digital values that a processor can read.
How It Works
An ADC:

samples the analog signal
measures its voltage
converts the measurement into a binary number

Sensor voltage
      ↓
     ADC
      ↓
Binary data
      ↓
Processor
Main Uses
ADCs are used with:

microphones
temperature sensors
pressure sensors
cameras

Resolution
Resolution determines how many digital levels the ADC can represent.
An n-bit ADC has:
2^n
possible output levels.
For example:
8-bit ADC  → 256 levels
10-bit ADC → 1024 levels
12-bit ADC → 4096 levels
Higher resolution allows smaller voltage differences to be measured.
DAC
DAC stands for Digital-to-Analog Converter.
It converts digital data into an analog voltage or current.
How It Works
A DAC receives a binary value and produces a corresponding analog output.
Digital data
      ↓
     DAC
      ↓
Analog voltage
      ↓
Speaker or circuit
Main Uses
DACs are used in:

audio systems
headphones
speakers
video equipment
motor control
signal generators

ADC vs. DAC

























ADCDACAnalog to digitalDigital to analogUsed for inputsUsed for outputsReads sensors and signalsDrives speakers and analog circuitsProduces binary dataProduces voltage or current

electrical-engineering/semiconductor/dig.title: Digital Logic Design
electrical-engineering/semiconductor/dig.content:
Digital logic design is the process of creating circuits that operate using binary values:
0 and 1
These circuits are built from components such as:

logic gates
multiplexers
registers
counters
state machines

RTL
RTL stands for Register-Transfer Level.
It describes how data moves between registers and what operations happen on each clock cycle.
For example:
Register A
    ↓
   ALU
    ↓
Register B
RTL is commonly written using hardware description languages such as:

Verilog
SystemVerilog
VHDL

Design Flow
Requirement Specification
     ↓
RTL Design
     ↓
Simulation and Verification
     ↓
Synthesis
     ↓
Physical chip implementation
Key Idea
Digital logic design creates hardware that works with binary signals.
RTL is a way to describe how data is stored, transferred, and processed inside that hardware.

electrical-engineering/semiconductor/dop.title: Doping
electrical-engineering/semiconductor/dop.content:
Doping is the process of adding a small amount of impurity atoms to a pure Semiconductor.
It changes the number of mobile electrons or holes and increases conductivity.
Doping creates two main semiconductor types:
Semiconductor
├── N-type → electrons are majority carriers
└── P-type → holes are majority carriers
N-Type Semiconductor
N-type silicon is created by adding atoms with five valence electrons, such as:

phosphorus
arsenic

Silicon has four valence electrons.
Four dopant electrons form bonds with nearby silicon atoms, leaving one extra electron that can move through the material.
Phosphorus added to silicon
            ↓
Four electrons form bonds
            ↓
One extra mobile electron
Therefore:

majority carriers: electrons
minority carriers: holes

The material is still electrically neutral overall.
P-Type Semiconductor
P-type silicon is created by adding atoms with three valence electrons, such as:

boron
gallium

Because one bond is incomplete, a hole is created.
Boron added to silicon
          ↓
One incomplete bond
          ↓
A hole is created
Nearby electrons can move into the hole, making the hole appear to move through the material.
Therefore:

majority carriers: holes
minority carriers: electrons

The material is still electrically neutral overall.
N-Type vs. P-Type

























N-TypeP-TypeExtra electronsMissing electrons create holesElectrons are majority carriersHoles are majority carriersUses donor atomsUses acceptor atomsCommon dopant: phosphorusCommon dopant: boron
Why Doping Is Important
Doping makes it possible to create:

Diode
Transistor
MOSFET
LEDs
solar cells
integrated circuits

Key Idea
Doping controls semiconductor conductivity by changing the number and type of charge carriers.
N-type material mainly conducts using electrons, while P-type material mainly conducts using holes.

electrical-engineering/semiconductor/eda.title: EDA Tools
electrical-engineering/semiconductor/eda.content:
EDA stands for Electronic Design Automation.
EDA tools are software used to design, simulate, verify, and analyze electronic circuits and semiconductor chips.
Common Uses

circuit simulation
RTL simulation
hardware verification
synthesis
timing analysis
PCB design
chip layout

Examples

LTspice
ModelSim / Questa
Synopsys VCS
Cadence Xcelium
Vivado
Quartus
Cadence Virtuoso

electrical-engineering/semiconductor/fee.title: Feedback System
electrical-engineering/semiconductor/fee.content:
A feedback system uses part of its output and sends it back to the input.
The feedback changes how the system behaves.
Input
  ↓
System
  ↓
Output
  ↓
Feedback
  └────→ back to input
Negative Feedback
Negative feedback subtracts part of the output from the input.
It is commonly used to:

stabilize gain
reduce distortion
reduce sensitivity to component variation
improve accuracy
increase bandwidth

Negative feedback is widely used in [op-amp] circuits.
Positive Feedback
Positive feedback adds part of the output back to the input.
It can make the output change more strongly.
It is commonly used in:

oscillators
comparators with hysteresis
switching circuits

Too much positive feedback can make a system unstable or cause oscillation.
Example
In an op-amp amplifier:
Input
  ↓
Op-Amp
  ↓
Output
  ↓
Feedback Network
  └────→ Input
The feedback network helps determine the closed-loop gain.
Key Idea
Feedback = using the output of a system to influence its input.

Negative feedback → usually improves stability and accuracy
Positive feedback → reinforces changes and can create switching or oscillation

electrical-engineering/semiconductor/har.title: Scripting Languages for Hardware Development
electrical-engineering/semiconductor/har.content:
Scripting languages are used to automate repetitive tasks in hardware design and verification.
They do not usually describe the hardware itself.
Instead, they help control tools, process files, generate tests, and analyze results.
Common Uses
Scripting languages are used for:

running simulations
processing log files
generating test data
automating builds
controlling EDA tools
analyzing verification results

Python
Python is commonly used for:

automation
data analysis
test generation
parsing simulation results
verification scripts

Tcl
Tcl stands for Tool Command Language.
It is commonly used to control EDA and FPGA tools.
For example, Tcl scripts can automate:

synthesis
timing analysis
FPGA builds
tool configuration

Perl
Perl is often found in older semiconductor and EDA workflows.
It is useful for:

text processing
log analysis
file generation
automation

HDL vs. Scripting Language





















HDLScripting LanguageDescribes hardwareAutomates engineering tasksVerilog, VHDL, SystemVerilogPython, Tcl, PerlUsed to create RTLUsed to control tools and workflows

electrical-engineering/semiconductor/hdl.title: Hardware Description Languages
electrical-engineering/semiconductor/hdl.content:
A Hardware Description Language, or HDL, is used to describe digital hardware.
Unlike normal programming languages, HDLs describe circuits that can operate in parallel.
HDLs are commonly used for:

digital logic design
RTL design
FPGA development
ASIC design
hardware simulation

VHDL
VHDL stands for VHSIC Hardware Description Language.
It is a strongly typed HDL commonly used in:

FPGA design
aerospace
defense
academic projects

Verilog
Verilog is an HDL used to describe digital circuits.
Its syntax is relatively similar to C, so it is often easier to read than VHDL.
It is widely used for:

RTL design
FPGA development
ASIC design

SystemVerilog
SystemVerilog is an extension of Verilog.
It adds more features for both hardware design and verification.
It supports:

RTL design
assertions
object-oriented programming
random testing
functional coverage
UVM

electrical-engineering/semiconductor/ic.title: IC (Integrated Circuit)
electrical-engineering/semiconductor/ic.content:
An integrated circuit, or IC, is a small electronic circuit built on a single piece of semiconductor material, usually silicon.
IC, Chip, and Semiconductor

Semiconductor

A material whose electrical conductivity can be controlled. Silicon is the most commonly used semiconductor material.


Integrated Circuit

An electronic circuit containing many components fabricated on a semiconductor material.


Chip

A common informal term for an integrated circuit or the small piece of silicon containing it.



Memory and Processing ICs
These ICs store data or process information.

NAND Flash
SoC
LPDDR
MCU

Power Management ICs
These ICs control voltage, current, charging, and power distribution.

Voltage Regulator
Charging IC

controls how electrical power is delivered to a rechargeable battery


PMIC

manages and distributes power inside an electronic device


Wireless Charging IC

controls the transfer of power without a physical cable connection
usually works using electromagnetic induction between two coils



Connectivity and Interface ICs
These ICs allow electronic devices to communicate with other devices or components.

Bluetooth IC
Wi-Fi Module
NFC Controller

Near Field Communication
manages very short-range wireless communication between nearby devices


UWB SoC

Ultra-Wideband
a chip designed for short-range communication and precise position measurement


USB-C Controller

Sensor ICs
These ICs detect changes in the physical environment.

Temperature Sensor IC
Accelerometer and Gyroscope

accelerometer detects linear movement, and gyroscope detects rotation



Audio and Input ICs
These ICs process audio signals or user input.

Audio Amplifier
Digitizer

converts touch or pen input into digital information (used in phones, and other touchscreen devices)



RF ICs and Modules
These components generate, amplify, transmit, or receive radio-frequency signals.

RF Transmitter
RF Front-End Module

controls and improves RF signals between the antenna and the communication system


Power Amplifier

Key Idea
Each semiconductor IC is designed for a specific function.
In an electronic device, multiple ICs work together. For example, a smartphone may use:

an SoC for processing
LPDDR for temporary memory
NAND Flash for storage
a PMIC for power management
Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, NFC, and UWB ICs for wireless communication
sensor ICs for motion and temperature detection
an audio amplifier for speaker output

electrical-engineering/semiconductor/ind.title: Semiconductor Industry
electrical-engineering/semiconductor/ind.content:
Digital systems ultimately process information using binary values: 0 and 1.
Electronic circuits can represent these values using switches that are either ON or OFF.
A transistor works like a very small electronic switch.
By placing billions of transistors on a small semiconductor chip, the chip can perform complex calculations, process information, and store data.
Main Types of Semiconductor Chips
Memory Semiconductor
Memory chips are mainly used to store information.
Examples:

DRAM
NAND Flash

Major companies:

Samsung Electronics
SK hynix

System Semiconductor
System semiconductors are mainly used to process information and perform calculations.
Examples:

CPU
GPU
AP
SoC

Major companies include:

Intel
AMD
NVIDIA

Semiconductor Company Types
IDM
IDM stands for Integrated Device Manufacturer.
An IDM company designs and manufactures its own semiconductor chips.
Examples:

Samsung Electronics
Intel
SK hynix

Design + Manufacturing
        ↓
       IDM
Fabless
A fabless company specializes mainly in semiconductor design.
It does not operate large-scale semiconductor manufacturing facilities.
Examples:

AMD
NVIDIA
Qualcomm

Chip Design
    ↓
Fabless Company
    ↓
Foundry Manufacturing
Foundry
A foundry manufactures semiconductor chips designed by other companies.
A major example is:

TSMC

TSMC is a Taiwanese semiconductor company and one of the world’s major semiconductor foundries.
Fab
A semiconductor manufacturing facility is commonly called a fab, short for fabrication facility.
A fab contains highly specialized equipment used to manufacture chips on silicon wafers.
ASML
ASML is a company that produces advanced equipment used in semiconductor manufacturing.
Its photolithography machines allow extremely small circuit patterns to be transferred onto wafers.
Smaller patterns make it possible to place more transistors in a limited chip area.
Simple Industry Structure
Fabless
  │
  │ designs chips
  ↓
Foundry
  │
  │ manufactures chips
  ↓
Finished Semiconductor Chip
An IDM performs both design and manufacturing within the same company.

electrical-engineering/semiconductor/mix.title: Mixed Signal
electrical-engineering/semiconductor/mix.content:
A mixed-signal circuit or IC contains both analog and digital circuits.
It is used when a digital system needs to interact with real-world analog signals.
Examples include:

audio systems
sensor interfaces
communication circuits
image sensors
data converters

Common Mixed-Signal Blocks

ADC
DAC
comparator
op-amp
PLL
sensor interface
analog front-end
digital control logic

Why It Is Important
Real-world signals are often analog, while processors and memory mainly operate digitally.
Mixed-signal circuits provide the interface between these two domains.
Key Idea
Mixed-signal = analog circuits + digital circuits working together in the same system or IC.
See also:

Signal
ADC
DAC

electrical-engineering/semiconductor/rip.title: Ripple
electrical-engineering/semiconductor/rip.content:
Ripple is a small unwanted variation in a DC voltage or current.
Instead of being perfectly constant, the signal slightly rises and falls over time.

Common Causes
Ripple commonly comes from:

rectifiers
switching regulators
power supplies
insufficient filtering

Ripple Voltage
Ripple is often measured using peak-to-peak voltage.
V_{\text{ripple(pp)}} = V_{\max} - V_{\min}
For example, if a 5 V supply varies between 4.95 V and 5.05 V:
V_{\text{ripple(pp)}} = 0.10V
Reducing Ripple
Ripple can be reduced using:

capacitors
LC filters
voltage regulators
proper PCB layout

Ripple vs. Noise

Ripple → usually periodic variation caused by power conversion
Noise → general unwanted electrical disturbance

Key Idea
Ripple is the small unwanted fluctuation that remains on top of a DC voltage or current.

electrical-engineering/semiconductor/sem.title: Semiconductor Manufacturing Process
electrical-engineering/semiconductor/sem.content:
Semiconductor manufacturing is the process of building extremely small electronic components on a silicon wafer.
The major manufacturing steps are often summarized as the 8 major semiconductor processes.
Wafer Manufacturing
  ↓
Oxidation
  ↓
Photolithography
  ↓
Etching
  ↓
Deposition & Ion Implantation
  ↓
Metal Wiring
  ↓
Electrical Die Sorting (EDS)
  ↓
Packaging.      
The first six steps are pre-process, where circuits are created on the wafer.
Testing and packaging are post-process, where individual chips are inspected, separated, and packaged.
1. Wafer Manufacturing
A wafer is a thin circular piece of semiconductor material, usually silicon.
A wafer is the foundation for the semiconductor. Most wafers are made of silicon extracted from sand. Sand is heated until it melts into a high purity liquid and then gets solidifed by crystalization. The resultant silicon rod is called an ingot(silicon pilar).
These ingots are sliced into a disc thinly sliced wafers.
The surface of sliced wafers is rough and contains defects so polishing machines are used to polish the surface of a wafer. The reason is that defects on the surface could negatively affect the precision of circuits.
Fun Fact: The word wafer comes from biscuit wafers because if you look at a photo of wafers, you can see a grid pattern on the surface.
A wafer made this way is the main material for semiconductors. The larger the diameter is, the greater the number of chips that can be produced per wafer, so the diameter of wafers is becoming larger.
Silicon → Ingot → Slice → Wafer
The wafer becomes the base on which transistors and circuits are built.
2. Oxidation
Oxidation creates a thin layer of silicon dioxide (SiO₂) on the wafer surface.
Oxygen or water vapor is sprayed on the wafer surface to form a uniform oxide film.
This oxide film protects the wafer surface during the following processes and also blocks current leakage between circuits.
The film acts as a strong protective shield.
This layer can be used as:

an electrical insulator
a protective layer
part of transistor structures

3. Photolithography
Photolithography draws a circuit design onto a wafer.
It is similar to developing a photo taken on a film camera. With semiconductors, a photomask functions as the film.
A photomask is a glass substrate with a computer-designed circuit pattern. In order to draw the circuit on the wafer, the photoresist,
a material that responds to light, is applied thinly and evenly on the oxide film previously placed on the wafer.
When light transfers the patterned photomask, the circuit is drawn on the wafer surface.
Just like developing a photo, a circuit pattern is imprinted on the wafer by spraying developer and removing unlit areas from the areas that are exposed to light.
After an inspection of the wafer to check whether the pattern is drawn well, it moves onto the next step.
Photoresist
    ↓
Mask + Light
    ↓
Circuit pattern on wafer
4. Etching
Etching removes unwanted material from the wafer.
The photoresist pattern protects areas that should remain.
Unnecessary materials are carved out, so that only the designed pattern remains.
Using a liquid or gas etchant, unnecessary materials are selectively removed to draw the desired design.
when chemical solutions are used for etching, it is called wet etching, and when gas or plasma ia used, it is called dry etching.

Pattern
   ↓
Etching
   ↓
Unwanted material removed
Common methods include:

wet etching
dry etching


5. Deposition and Ion Implantation
Deposition
Deposition adds extremely thin layers of material onto the wafer.
It’s like constructing a building on a semiconductor chip, samller than a fingernail and thinner than a sheet of paper.
The photolithography process and the etching process are repeated several times on the wafer, layer by layer.
An insulating film that separates and protects the stacked circuits is required. that’s called a thin film.
Coating the thin film at a desired molecular or atomic level onto a wafer is called deposition.
Since the coating is so thin, precise and sophisticated technology is required to uniformly apply the thin film on a wafer.
These layers may include:

insulators
conductors
semiconductor materials


Ion Implantation
Ion implantation adds impurity atoms to silicon.
To give the semiconductor electrical characteristics, ion implementation is also required.
A semiconductor made of silicon does not conduct electricity, but adding impurities, it conducts current and has conductive properties.
After all these processes, the wafer becomes conductive and numerous circuits are drawn on it.
This process is called Doping.
Ion implantation creates:

N-type regions
P-type regions

These regions are necessary for building transistors.

6. Metal Interconnection
Metal wires are created on the chip to connect transistors and other components.
In order for this circuit to work, an electrical signal must be applied.
it is necessary to create a path for electricity to pass through according to the circuit pattern.
This process is called the metal wiring process. It is a process that allows electricity to flow by forming thin metal layers
using materials such as aluminum, titanium, or tungsten, so that electricity can pass through the semiconductor well.
Copper is commonly used for these connections.
Transistor ── Metal wire ── Transistor
Modern chips contain many layers of metal interconnections.
7. Testing
The manufactured chips are electrically tested.
EDS (Electrical Die Sorting): the process of testing electrical characteristics to make sure each individual chip has reached the desired quality level, simply, it is a testing step to sort out defective chips
Yield
Yield represents the percentage of usable chips produced from a wafer.
\text{Yield}
=
\frac{\text{Number of Working Chips}}
{\text{Total Number of Chips}}
\times 100
A higher yield means more functional chips are produced from each wafer.
Testing checks whether:

transistors work correctly
circuits produce the expected output
defective chips can be identified

Testing may occur both before and after packaging.
8. Packaging
Packaging converts individual semiconductor dies into finished chips that can be installed in electronic devices.
The wafer completed in the previous steps are cut into individual semiconductor chips that can be loaded on an electronic device.
This is called wafer sawing or dicing.
Wafer
   ↓
Dicing
   ↓
Individual Die
   ↓
Package
A typical packaging process includes:
Wafer Sawing / Dicing
        ↓
Die Attach (placed on PCB board)
        ↓
Wire Bonding
        ↓
Molding
        ↓
Marking
        ↓
Final Test
Die Attach
The semiconductor die is attached to a package substrate.
Wire Bonding
Contact point of the semiconductor chip is placed on a substrate is connected with the contact point of the substrate
Molding
The chip is enclosed in protective material.
This protects the semiconductor from:

moisture
dust
mechanical damage
external contamination

Marking
Information such as the product name or identification code is printed on the package.
Final Test
The packaged semiconductor is tested again to make sure it operates correctly.
Key Idea
Semiconductor manufacturing repeatedly creates, removes, and modifies extremely thin layers on a silicon wafer.
Create wafer
→ build layers
→ pattern layers
→ remove material
→ dope silicon
→ connect devices
→ test
→ package
These processes allow billions of transistors to be manufactured on a single chip.

electrical-engineering/semiconductor/ind.title: Semiconductor
electrical-engineering/semiconductor/ind.content:
A semiconductor is a material whose electrical conductivity can be controlled.
It behaves between a conductor and an insulator.
Bandgap
The bandgap is the energy required for an electron to move from the valence band to the conduction band.
E_g=E_C-E_V
where:

EC is the conduction-band edge
EV is the valence-band edge

An electron can conduct electricity after gaining enough energy to cross the bandgap.
Material Classification

























MaterialBandgapElectrical BehaviorConductorVery small or noneElectrons move easilySemiconductorSmallConductivity can be controlledInsulatorLargeVery little current flows
Examples:

conductors: copper, silver, aluminum
semiconductors: silicon, germanium, gallium arsenide
insulators: glass, rubber, ceramics

Conductivity
Semiconductor conductivity depends on the number and mobility of electrons and holes.
\sigma=q(n\mu_n+p\mu_p)
where:

n is the electron concentration
p is the hole concentration
μn is electron mobility
μp is hole mobility

Conductivity can be controlled using Doping.
PN Junction
A PN junction is formed when P-type and N-type semiconductor regions are joined.
P-type | Depletion region | N-type
holes  | few mobile       | electrons
       | carriers         |
Electrons and holes recombine near the junction, creating a depletion region and an internal electric field.
PN junctions are used in:

diodes
transistors
LEDs
solar cells
photodiodes
integrated circuits

Common Semiconductor Materials
Silicon
Silicon is the most widely used semiconductor.
It is used in:

CPUs
memory
sensors
power devices
integrated circuits

Its bandgap is approximately:
E_g\approx1.12\text{ eV}
Germanium
Germanium has high carrier mobility but also higher leakage current than silicon.
It is used in:

SiGe transistors
high-speed circuits
infrared detectors

Its bandgap is approximately:
E_g\approx0.66\text{ eV}
Gallium Arsenide
Gallium arsenide, or GaAs, has high electron mobility and good high-frequency performance.
It is used in:

RF amplifiers
radar
satellite communication
LEDs
laser diodes

Silicon Carbide
Silicon carbide, or SiC, is a wide-bandgap semiconductor used in high-voltage and high-power systems.
Common applications include:

electric vehicles
fast chargers
solar inverters
motor drives

Gallium Nitride
Gallium nitride, or GaN, is a wide-bandgap semiconductor with high switching speed.
It is used in:

compact chargers
RF power amplifiers
wireless base stations
power converters

Key Idea
A semiconductor has a controllable conductivity.
Its behavior can be changed using energy, temperature, electric fields, and doping.

electrical-engineering/semiconductor/sig.title: Analog/Digital Signals
electrical-engineering/semiconductor/sig.content:
Electronic systems represent information using analog or digital signals.
Analog Signal
An analog signal changes continuously over time.
It can have any value within a range.
Examples include:

sound from a microphone
temperature
light intensity
pressure
battery voltage

Voltage
  │      /‾\      /‾\
  │     /   \____/   \
  │____/______________\___ Time
A real-world signal is often analog because physical quantities change continuously.
Digital Signal
A digital signal uses separate values instead of a continuous range.
In digital electronics, information is usually represented using two states:
0 and 1
These states are represented by voltage ranges.
For example:
Low voltage  → 0
High voltage → 1
Voltage
  │    ┌─────┐       ┌─────┐
  │    │     │       │     │
  │____┘     └_______┘     └___ Time
Digital signals are used by:

computers
CPUs
MCUs
memory
communication systems

Analog vs. Digital

























AnalogDigitalChanges continuouslyUses discrete valuesCan have many possible valuesUsually represented by 0 and 1Common in real-world signalsCommon inside computersMore directly affected by noiseEasier to store and process reliably
Conversion
An ADC converts an analog signal into digital data.
Analog signal → ADC → Digital data
A DAC converts digital data into an analog signal.
Digital data → DAC → Analog signal
Example
In a digital audio system:
Sound
  ↓
Microphone
  ↓
Analog signal
  ↓
ADC
  ↓
Digital processing
  ↓
DAC
  ↓
Analog signal
  ↓
Speaker

electrical-engineering/semiconductor/soc.title: SoC
electrical-engineering/semiconductor/soc.content:
SoC stands for System on a Chip.
It combines many components of a computer or electronic system into a single integrated circuit.
Common Components
An SoC may include:

CPU
GPU
memory controller
communication interfaces
image processor
audio processor
security hardware
input and output controllers

Main Uses

smartphones
tablets
smartwatches
embedded systems
automobiles
IoT devices

Why SoCs Are Used
Integrating many components into one chip can make a device:

smaller
more power-efficient
faster
cheaper to manufacture

Examples
Smartphone SoCs include:

Apple A-series
Qualcomm Snapdragon
Samsung Exynos
MediaTek Dimensity

These chips combine processing, graphics, communication, and other functions into one package.
SoC vs. MCU

























SoCMCUDesigned for complex systemsDesigned for simpler control tasksOften runs a full operating systemOften runs firmware or a real-time operating systemUsually has powerful CPU and GPU coresUsually has lower processing powerCommon in smartphones and computersCommon in embedded control systems
Key Idea
An SoC places most of the major functions of an electronic system onto a single chip.
This reduces size and power consumption while allowing different components to communicate quickly.

electrical-engineering/semiconductor/sti.title: Stimulus
electrical-engineering/semiconductor/sti.content:
In hardware simulation and verification, a stimulus is an input or set of inputs applied to a circuit to test how it responds.
Examples include:

voltage signals
clock signals
reset signals
digital input patterns
test data

Example
Stimulus
   ↓
Design Under Test
   ↓
Output Response
For example, a testbench may apply different input values to a digital circuit and check whether the outputs are correct.
Key Idea
Stimulus = test input given to a circuit or hardware design.

electrical-engineering/semiconductor/top.title: Topology
electrical-engineering/semiconductor/top.content:
In circuit design, topology means the overall structure of a circuit and how its components are connected.
It describes the type of circuit arrangement, not the exact component values.
Examples
Common amplifier topologies include:

Common-Source Amplifier
Source Follower
Differential Amplifier
Telescopic Cascode
Folded Cascode
Two-Stage Amplifier

Different topologies have different characteristics such as:

gain
bandwidth
power consumption
output swing
noise
stability

Example
Two amplifiers may use different transistor sizes but still have the same topology if their connection structure is the same.
Same connection structure
        ↓
Same topology
Key Idea
Topology = how the circuit is structurally connected.
The topology determines the basic behavior and trade-offs of a circuit.

electrical-engineering/semiconductor/uvm.title: UVM
electrical-engineering/semiconductor/uvm.content:
UVM stands for Universal Verification Methodology.
It is a standardized method for verifying digital hardware using SystemVerilog.
Main Purpose
UVM helps engineers build reusable and organized test environments for complex hardware designs.
Common Components

Sequence

Generates test operations.


Driver

Sends inputs to the hardware design.


Monitor

Observes signals and outputs.


Scoreboard

Compares actual results with expected results.



Simple Flow
Sequence
   ↓
Driver
   ↓
Design Under Test
   ↓
Monitor
   ↓
Scoreboard
Key Idea
UVM provides a standard structure for testing and verifying digital hardware before it is manufactured.
